name: Hassan Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I'm not sure I'll be much use, I don't really follow the computer stuff. But go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter's mate on a roofing and repairs crew in a seaside town, four of us in an old white van. We strip old roofs, put in new rafters where the rot's got in, batten and felt, and the slater does the tiles. I carry, cut battens, and keep the scaffold tidy. I like being up high on a clear day looking at the sea; I don't like November, when the wind comes sideways off the water.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady is the work through the year?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Summer's mad, everyone wants their roof done before the storms. Winter, the boss lays two of us off for six to eight weeks, and I'm one of the two. I live with my girlfriend Lena, she works the tills at the supermarket, and we've got maybe a fortnight of money saved by October and nothing by February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought a computer was going to fix a roof. At work we'd have a laugh about it. I don't go online much, so I'd probably say nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means another winter laid off, same as every year. Nothing about AI was ever going to change the wind in November. That's the part that actually gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always: work every hour in summer, put a bit away, and sign on for the winter weeks. I'd ask the boss again if he'll keep me on through winter for indoor jobs, kitchens, skirting, whatever. And we'd cut back from October, no takeaways, no pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worn down, I suppose. Every year I tell myself I'll save more in summer and every year the car needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did last winter actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven weeks off. Lena picked up extra shifts, I did a few days helping my dad on his fishing boat for cash, and we were still short on the gas. I sold my old games console in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays small, is there anything you'd change about your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I'd like to get my roofing card one day, but the course is in the city, two hours away. I keep meaning to go.

say: I'd say I **never thought** a computer would fix a roof.
I'd have a **laugh** about it at work and stay quiet online.
think: AI flopping means another **winter laid off**, same as every year.
The **November wind**, not technology, is what costs him work.
do: Work **every summer hour** and sign on for the winter weeks.
Ask the boss for **indoor winter work** like kitchens and skirting.
feel: **Worn down** by the yearly cycle of summer promises and winter shortfall.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI was ever going to change the wind in November.
fieldNote: His **seasonal lay-off** is the dominant pressure, AI or not.
Last winter he **sold his console** and still came up short on gas.
He's **pragmatic**, without blame or politics.
His roofing card stays a **someday** plan because of distance.

steps.text: Ask the boss for indoor kitchen and skirting work through winter
Stop takeaways and pub nights from October
Help his dad on the fishing boat for cash in winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the office people, glad I work outside. At work the boss would say he'll use it for quotes, and I'd say fine, as long as it's not me getting quoted out. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it doesn't touch me directly for a while. But Lena's tills are going self-service already, and if her hours drop we're in real trouble. My girlfriend's shifts on the tills are what carry us through my winters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena to ask for the stockroom or the deli counter, somewhere a machine won't reach soon. We'd try harder to save in summer, maybe two hundred a month into a separate account. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff myself; the boss can do his quotes on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, worried for Lena. More worried for her than me, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your winters if Lena's hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to find winter work away from the roofs, maybe the council's road crew, gritting and potholes. I asked once and they said come back in September. I never did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you blame if it went that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Shops will always go for the cheaper option, same as my boss would if a robot did battens. It's just how it goes.

say: I'd say I'm **glad I work outside**.
I'd let the boss use AI for **quotes**, as long as I'm not quoted out.
think: His roofing job is **untouched** for a while.
His girlfriend's **supermarket tills** are going self-service, and her shifts carry his winters.
do: Urge his girlfriend to move to the **stockroom or deli**.
Save **two hundred** a month in summer.
Apply to the **council road crew** for winter gritting work.
feel: **Uneasy** for himself and more **worried** for his girlfriend.
S1.quote: My girlfriend's shifts on the tills are what carry us through my winters.
fieldNote: The household risk is in his **partner's checkout job**, not his roofing.
He **blames no one**, seeing it as how business goes.
He'd avoid using **AI himself** entirely.
He finally considers acting on the **council job** he once ignored.

steps.text: Put two hundred a month into savings each summer
Apply to the council road crew for winter gritting work
Help his girlfriend ask for a move to the stockroom or deli

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. At work we'd say the robots will fall off the scaffold. I'd still say nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's true, I'm finished. By 2031 a robot carries battens and nails felt better than me, and Lena's tills went years before that. We'd have no money, no papers and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the boss does first, because I can't afford to throw away the job I've got. I'd go back to the council about road work, and I'd talk to my dad about working on his boat full time. If we had to, we'd move into my parents' spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like standing on the ridge and feeling the ladder go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Is that really the plan, with only three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds daft. But I can't jump to nothing, and I don't know where to jump to. My boss doesn't know either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for your crew in the first three years, from 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss's quotes and the ordering would all be done by computer, so he'd run the van with fewer people. Maybe three of us instead of four. I'm the newest, so you can guess.

say: I'd say I **don't believe it** until I see it.
I'd joke the robots will **fall off** the scaffold.
think: By **2031** a robot carries battens and nails felt better than him.
His girlfriend's **tills** go years earlier, leaving no money and no papers.
do: **Wait to see** what the boss does before risking his job.
Go back to the **council** about road work.
Move into his **parents' spare room** if money runs out.
feel: **Sick**, like standing on the ridge and feeling the **ladder go**.
S2.quote: I can't jump to nothing, and I don't know where to jump to.
fieldNote: His **wait-and-see** is paralysis, not calm, and he knows it.
He expects the crew to shrink from **four to three** by 2028.
Both household earners are **exposed** within three years.
His fallback is **family**: the boat and his parents' spare room.

steps.text: Watch what the roofing boss does before quitting anything
Apply again to the council road crew
Ask his dad for full-time work on the fishing boat
Move into his parents' spare room if rent can't be paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get ready, so people should. At work I'd probably say we're fine till 2034. Online, still nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three is better, but I'm not good at using time. I've had years to get my roofing card. I just haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This time I'd actually go to the roofing course in the city, even if I have to sleep on my cousin's sofa for the week. I'd get Lena to look at a care-home job, because people will still want a person there. And I'd try to get on the council list for any steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but there's a gap to squeeze through now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at using time. What would make this time different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being scared, probably. Nothing gets me moving like the gas bill. If I knew robots were coming in 2034, that'd be a gas bill the size of a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Lena react to moving to care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say it's harder for the same money. And she'd be right. But she'd do it if it kept us going.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to get ready, so people should.
I'd tell the crew we're **fine till 2034**.
think: The longer runway is better, but he's **bad at using time**.
He's had years to get his **roofing card** and hasn't.
do: Attend the **roofing course** in the city, staying on his cousin's sofa.
Get on the **council list** for steady jobs.
feel: **Scared**, but with a **gap** to squeeze through now.
S3.quote: Nothing gets me moving like the gas bill.
fieldNote: He knows his own **procrastination** is the risk.
Fear is his only **motivator**, and he says so.
His girlfriend would take **harder care work** for the same pay.
Mood stays alarmed: both incomes are **expected to go**.

steps.text: Take the roofing card course in the city
Put his name on the council's list for steady jobs
Help his girlfriend apply for care-home work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's ages, we'll sort something. At work it'd be a joke for a week and then forgotten. I wouldn't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably forget about it too, and that's the danger. Thirteen years till robots on roofs, I'd be forty. Enough time to sort something, if I'm not lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the roofing card, finally. I'd keep summers full and save. I'd probably wait to see what other roofers do before going further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad. A little worried that I'll waste it, like I waste every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might forget. What would remind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, probably. She's the organised one. She'd put it on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own small crew, maybe, doing the old houses robots won't understand. Crooked chimneys, rotten valleys. Nobody's robot is building a crooked chimney.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages and we'll sort something.
It'd be a **joke for a week** at work and then forgotten.
think: He might **forget** about it too, and that's the danger.
**Thirteen years** to robots gives him time if he's not lazy.
do: **Wait to see** what other roofers do before going further.
feel: **Not bad**, but worried he'll **waste** the time like his winters.
S4.quote: Nobody's robot is building a crooked chimney.
fieldNote: A long warning risks making him **complacent**, and he admits it.
His **girlfriend** is the organiser who would keep him on track.
He dreams of a small crew doing **awkward old roofs**.
Seasonal **winter gaps** keep him anxious regardless of AI.

steps.text: Finally finish the roofing card course in the city
Save from every full summer week
Watch what other roofers do before changing anything else

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Lena's tills and my roofs, both gone in three years, and nowhere round here to go. What would help is somebody paying for the roofing course and a winter wage so I'm not on the dole every January.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the seaside. Half the houses in my seaside town are holiday lets now, empty all winter. If they stopped getting their roofs done, we'd all be out anyway.

headlineQuote: Half the houses in my seaside town are holiday lets now, empty all winter.
portrait: Hassan is **27**, a carpenter's mate on a **seaside roofing** crew, laid off every winter.
He's **pragmatic**, avoids AI tools and blames no one, seeing cuts as how business goes.
His girlfriend's **supermarket tills** are the household's most exposed income.
AGI by **2028** leaves him frozen, waiting to see with no plan.
With more time he'd finally take his **roofing card**, though he fears wasting it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household jobs gone in three years.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **roofing course** and a **winter wage** to stop the yearly dole.
